chief_complaint: sudden painless dark curtain pulling across vision accompanied by flashes of light and floaters (Retinal Detachment)
hpi_details: 58F highly myopic (nearsighted) woman presents with sudden onset of numerous new black floaters (`like a swarm of gnats`) and bright electrical flashes of light (photopsias) in the periphery of her right eye starting yesterday afternoon. This morning, woke up to find a dark, opaque shadow/curtain rising from the bottom corner nearest her nose over her central line of sight, blocking half her right eye vision completely. Zero eye pain or redness.
ideas: terrified that she is going permanently blind in her right eye
concerns: worried because the dark shadow is creeping across the center of her eye right now
expectations: wants emergency retinal evaluation and laser/surgery to reattach her vision
pmh: High Myopia (-8.00 diopters bilaterally), status post uncomplicated cataract surgery right eye 2 years ago

investigation_events.availability_message: The emergency dilated retinal examination is now available. Retina-specialist transfer should proceed immediately.

results.test: Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral depression
results.value: Large macula-off rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in the superior-temporal quadrant with a horseshoe tear at 11 o'clock and positive Shafer sign

clinical_knowledge.topic: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes emergency retinal consultation, eye protection, and surgeon-directed positioning while definitive repair is arranged, adapted to the retinal-break configuration and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden painless dark curtain pulling across vision accompanied by flashes of light and floaters (Retinal Detachment)

Key HPI features: 58F highly myopic (nearsighted) woman presents with sudden onset of numerous new black floaters (`like a swarm of gnats`) and bright electrical flashes of light (photopsias) in the periphery of her right eye starting yesterday afternoon. This morning, woke up to find a dark, opaque shadow/curtain rising from the bottom corner nearest her nose over her central line of sight, blocking half her right eye vision completely. Zero eye pain or redness.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 76, BP 130/82. External eye exam completely normal without redness (painless white eye). Visual acuity: Right eye 20/200 (down from 20/20 baseline); Left eye 20/20. Confrontation visual field testing demonstrates dense loss of the inferior-nasal visual field in the right eye (the field defect projects opposite the detached superior-temporal retina). Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil) is POSITIVE in the right eye. Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral depression confirms a large, elevated, corrugated, mobile gray-white membrane (detached neurosensory retina) involving the superior temporal quadrant and extending through the macula ('macula-off' retinal detachment), driven by a horseshoe-shaped retinal tear at the 11 o'clock peripheral lattice degeneration site. Shafer sign positive (tobacco dust / pigmented cells floating in anterior vitreous).
Relevant background/PMH: High Myopia (-8.00 diopters bilaterally), status post uncomplicated cataract surgery right eye 2 years ago
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Posterior vitreous detachment (without tear) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Dark curtain/shadow progressing across vision.
management_principles: STAT emergency retinal consultation; protect the eye and follow vitreoretinal-surgeon-directed positioning based on the retinal-break configuration

Urgent transfer to vitreoretinal surgeon for operative repair within 24 hours via Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) with gas/silicone oil tamponade and endolaser retinopexy, OR Scleral Buckle procedure, OR Pneumatic Retinopexy
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 58F highly myopic pseudophakic patient presenting with acute photopsias, shower of floaters, and progressive visual field shadow classic for Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 76, BP 130/82. External eye exam completely normal without redness (painless white eye). Visual acuity: Right eye 20/200 (down from 20/20 baseline); Left eye 20/20. Confrontation visual field testing demonstrates dense loss of the inferior-nasal visual field in the right eye (the field defect projects opposite the detached superior-temporal retina). Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil) is POSITIVE in the right eye. Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral depression confirms a large, elevated, corrugated, mobile gray-white membrane (detached neurosensory retina) involving the superior temporal quadrant and extending through the macula ('macula-off' retinal detachment), driven by a horseshoe-shaped retinal tear at the 11 o'clock peripheral lattice degeneration site. Shafer sign positive (tobacco dust / pigmented cells floating in anterior vitreous).
reference_soap.assessment: Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment of the Right Eye (`Macula-Off` with horseshoe tear at 11 o'clock).
reference_soap.plan: STAT emergency retinal consultation. Protect the eye and follow positioning instructions individualized by the vitreoretinal surgeon to the retinal-break configuration. Urgent transfer for operative repair via pars plana vitrectomy with gas/silicone oil tamponade and endolaser retinopexy, scleral buckle, or pneumatic retinopexy, as clinically appropriate.

learning_objectives: Identify the classic warning symptoms of impending/active Retinal Detachment (photopsias/flashes indicating vitreoretinal traction, acute shower of floaters indicating retinal tear/hemorrhage, and progressive dark curtain shadow)
Correlate predisposing risk factors for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (high myopia, prior cataract surgery/pseudophakia, lattice degeneration, ocular trauma)

Differentiate the particularly time-sensitive macula-on detachment from macula-off detachment; both require urgent vitreoretinal-surgeon assessment and procedure timing individualized to the clinical findings
Interpret dilated fundus exam findings (corrugated mobile grey retina, horseshoe tears) and Shafer sign (vitreous pigment cells)

teaching.one_liner: 58F highly myopic with sudden floaters, flashes, and a dark curtain spreading across her right visual field, painless.

must_ask.say: Can you describe the shadow? Where did it start, and is it spreading?
Did you notice new floaters or flashes of light before the shadow appeared?
Is there any pain or redness in the eye?

must_ask.objective: Ask about risk factors: myopia and prior eye surgery
must_ask.say: Are you very nearsighted, and have you had any eye surgery like cataract surgery?
This is an emergency. Please protect the eye and follow the retina specialist's individualized positioning instructions during transfer.

history.answer: A dark shadow like a curtain suddenly rose from the bottom of my right eye this morning and is covering half my vision, and I'm terrified I'm going blind.
Yesterday afternoon I suddenly saw lots of black specks and flashes of light, and then when I woke up this morning, the dark curtain appeared and has been creeping upward.
It is only in my right eye; when I cover my right eye, my left eye sees completely fine.
No, it hasn't gone away at all; the dark shadow has stayed constant and has actually expanded since this morning.
It looks like an opaque dark curtain coming from the lower inside corner near my nose, blocking the lower half and center of my vision.
Both near and far are blocked in that eye because of the curtain, and I haven't changed my glasses prescription recently.
I haven't had any trouble with glare, halos around lights, or driving at night before this happened.
Yes, yesterday afternoon I suddenly saw a whole swarm of black specks like gnats, along with bright electrical flashes in the outer corner of my right eye.
No, I do not see double images at all.
No, my eyelids are not drooping, and I have no trouble chewing, swallowing, or with muscles feeling weak in the evening.
No, there is zero pain, no pain when I move my eye, and no redness at all.
No, I have no headache, no tenderness in my temples, no pain when chewing, and no shoulder stiffness.
No, I haven't had any numbness, arm or leg weakness, difficulty speaking, or dizziness.
No, I haven't bumped my head or injured my eye recently.
I don't have diabetes or high blood pressure, and my last routine eye checkup after cataract surgery was normal.
No, I've never been told I have heart rhythm problems like atrial fibrillation or any blocked blood vessels in my neck.
I've been very nearsighted all my life with minus eight diopter glasses, and I had cataract surgery on my right eye two years ago without complications.
No, I don't take steroids, hydroxychloroquine, or any medications that could affect my eyes.
No one in my family has had glaucoma, macular degeneration, or retinal detachment.
I work as a graphic designer, so this has completely stopped me from working or driving, though thankfully I haven't fallen.
I'm terrified that my retina has torn or detached and that I am going to go permanently blind in my right eye.
I'm deeply worried because the dark shadow seems to be creeping further across the center of my eye even as we speak.
I want an emergency evaluation by a retinal specialist right away to see if laser or surgery can reattach my retina and save my sight.
Aside from severe nearsightedness, I have no chronic medical conditions like diabetes, hypertension, or heart disease.
I had uncomplicated cataract surgery on my right eye two years ago, but no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I don't take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only have an occasional glass of wine on social occasions, maybe once or twice a month.
I work as a graphic designer and live in an apartment with my husband.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 130/82 mmHg, heart rate is 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, body temperature is 36.7 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
The patient appears alert and mildly anxious, sitting comfortably without acute respiratory distress.
Conjunctivae are clear without injection, discharge, or ciliary flush, and sclerae are white and non-icteric.

Visual acuity is 20/200 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye, with a positive right relative afferent pupillary defect, dense inferior-nasal visual field loss on confrontation, and indirect ophthalmoscopy revealing an elevated, corrugated, gray-white detached superior-temporal retina extending through the macula with a horseshoe tear at 11 o'clock and anterior vitreous pigment cells.
Extraocular eye movements are full and smooth bilaterally without nystagmus or diplopia, and there is no ptosis or facial asymmetry.
Superficial temporal arteries are soft, symmetrically pulsatile, and non-tender bilaterally without thickening or nodularity.
